summary: Describes how EAP-FAST can be used to provision credentials and other information to a peer through its TLS-protected tunnel. This is an informational document, later updated by RFC 8996.

eli5.summary: After building a safe tube between two computers, one side hands the other the keys or settings it will need later, with nobody else able to see.

questions: what is a pac in eap-fast
how does eap-fast prevent man in the middle during provisioning
subtitle: How EAP-FAST uses its TLS tunnel to hand a device the credentials it needs, with or without proving the server first.

tldr.problem: EAP-FAST needs a peer to hold credentials such as a pre-shared key, a certificate trust anchor or a Protected Access Credential (PAC) before it can mutually authenticate with a server, and getting them onto devices is a deployment hurdle.
tldr.mechanism: The peer and server build a TLS tunnel, run an inner authentication such as EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2, check the tunnel with a Crypto-Binding TLV, and only then send the PAC or trusted root certificate through the tunnel. The tunnel is either server-authenticated or anonymous.
tldr.outcome: Server-authenticated provisioning is the recommended mode and gives much better protection against man-in-the-middle attacks. The anonymous mode allows zero-touch setup but is exposed to offline dictionary attacks. RFC 8996 later updated this document.

today: RFC 5422 is an Informational RFC and was updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted. The IESG note in the text says it documents existing EAP-FAST use to promote interoperability.

sections.title: Why Provision Over the Tunnel
sections.content:
EAP-FAST (RFC 4851) is an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that can mutually authenticate a peer and a server. Before that works, the peer must already have credentials: a pre-shared key, a certificate trust anchor, or a Protected Access Credential (PAC). Provisioning these is often a deployment obstacle.

This document describes how EAP-FAST can provision them dynamically and in-band, through the protected TLS tunnel (RFC 5246). An IESG note says EAP-FAST had been implemented by many vendors and used in the Internet, and that publication is meant to promote interoperability by documenting current use.

The note also says EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2 reuses the EAP type code 26 assigned to EAP-MSCHAPv2, but with changes that make it not interoperable with plain EAP-MSCHAPv2. Assigned method types must not be re-used with different meaning inside tunneled methods in the future.
sections.eli5: A club card lets you into the club, but first someone must give you the card. This paper is about giving out the card through a secret tunnel, so nobody has to carry it over by hand.

sections.title: The Two Provisioning Modes
sections.content:
Provisioning happens in phase 2, inside a TLS tunnel that phase 1 set up. There are two modes.

  • Server-Authenticated Provisioning Mode. The peer has already authenticated the server during tunnel setup. The server MAY then authenticate the peer inside the tunnel before it provisions anything. Implementations MUST support the ciphersuites TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, and the peer MUST validate the server's certificate chain.
  • Server-Unauthenticated Provisioning Mode. The tunnel is anonymous. The peer signals this by negotiating an anonymous Diffie-Hellman ciphersuite, and implementations MUST support TLS_DH_anon_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. Both sides must contribute to the key, so RSA key transport MUST NOT be used. Anonymous modes MUST support the 2048-bit group 14 from RFC 3526.

The unauthenticated mode exists to bootstrap peers that lack strong credentials. Because an attacker could intercept the tunnel, the peer and server MUST complete a mutually authenticating inner EAP method with key derivation, and the peer then uses the Crypto-Binding TLV to check that the tunnel was not subject to a man-in-the-middle attack.

The server-authenticated mode is recommended, and a peer MUST use it whenever it holds a valid trust root for the server.
sections.eli5: Either you check the stranger's ID before talking, or you talk first and test them with a secret handshake afterward. Checking the ID first is much safer.

sections.title: The Provisioning Conversation
sections.content:
The steps are: build the phase 1 tunnel, run an inner EAP method, exchange the Crypto-Binding TLV, provision the credential, and finish with Result TLVs as defined in RFC 4851. The server provisions credentials only after authentication and a successful Crypto-Binding exchange. The peer can ask for a PAC or the server can send it unsolicited. The Result TLV MUST precede the TLVs to be provisioned, and a PAC TLV MUST NOT be accepted outside an encrypted TLS tunnel.

For the anonymous mode, the inner method is EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2, which implementations MUST support. It was chosen partly because its hash-based challenge-response slows an active attack and gives some ability to detect a man-in-the-middle. With an anonymous Diffie-Hellman exchange, the challenges come from TLS key material (an extra 72 octets from the end of the key_block, including a 40-octet session_key_seed and two 16-octet challenges) instead of from the exchanged messages, which are zeroed on sending and ignored on receipt. In server-authenticated mode, EAP-FAST-GTC and EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2 MUST both be supported.

Afterward, network access is up to server policy. At the end of an unauthenticated provisioning exchange, access SHOULD NOT be granted, and the server SHOULD end with an EAP Failure. Since a failure can disrupt devices such as 802.11 clients, the RFC suggests TLS renegotiation using the new credentials as a smoother route to the next authentication.
sections.eli5: First the two sides build the tube. Then they prove who they are in a way that fits the tube. Only then does the server pass over the key, and the other side says thanks.

sections.title: What Gets Provisioned and the TLV Formats
sections.content:
A PAC is a credential the server generates for a peer. It travels in a PAC TLV (TLV type 11), which carries a list of PAC attributes, each a 2-octet type and a 2-octet length followed by a value. The attribute types are PAC-Key (1), PAC-Opaque (2), PAC-Lifetime (3), A-ID (4), I-ID (5), A-ID-Info (7), PAC-Acknowledgement (8), PAC-Info (9) and PAC-Type (10).

  • PAC-Key is a randomly generated secret of 32 octets.
  • PAC-Opaque is data the peer MUST NOT interpret. The server generates it and protects it cryptographically. The peer stores it per issuing authority and presents it back, for a Tunnel PAC in the ClientHello SessionTicket extension (RFC 5077).
  • PAC-Info MUST contain the A-ID, A-ID-Info and PAC-Type. The A-ID identifies the issuing authority and it is RECOMMENDED to be 16 octets long.

Three PAC types exist. A peer requests one by sending a PAC TLV with the matching PAC Type. For a Tunnel PAC it MUST send a PAC-Acknowledgement TLV to confirm receipt, with result 1 for success or 2 for failure, and it MUST NOT use that TLV for other types.

A server can also deliver a trusted root certificate. The peer sends a Server-Trusted-Root TLV (type 18) and the server answers with a PKCS#7 TLV (type 20) containing a certificate or chain. The peer SHOULD authenticate the server before accepting a trusted server root certificate.
sections.eli5: A PAC is like a sealed envelope with a secret key stuck to it. You keep the envelope without opening it, and later show it to the server, which knows how to open it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document shares the security considerations of RFC 4851. Server-authenticated mode protects strongly against man-in-the-middle attacks, but it requires secure pre-provisioning of trust roots, which can be hard. The unauthenticated mode lets an attacker sit in the middle of the TLS handshake. It reduces the risk by tying the inner challenges to the TLS exchange and by Crypto-Binding. The RFC recommends that any other inner method resist attack at least as well as EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2, and cleartext passwords MUST NOT be used in this mode.

Both online and offline dictionary attacks are discussed. Server-authenticated mode mitigates offline attacks because the peer will not start phase 2 before authenticating the server. The unauthenticated mode is vulnerable to them. Implementations SHOULD log odd failures during phase 2 and warn the user, and may limit where the mode can be used.

Other points: a User Authorization PAC is a bearer credential with no key, so it MUST NOT be sent in the clear. A Machine Authentication PAC has a PAC-Key that MUST be kept secret. Both peer and server must store PAC material securely. The unauthenticated mode SHOULD be avoided where possible, but it is the only option enabling zero-touch provisioning.
sections.eli5: Skipping the ID check is easier but riskier, so the paper lists ways to catch tricksters and says to lock the keys in a safe place.

items.label: Tunnel PAC
items.desc: Secret key and opaque data used to establish the EAP-FAST tunnel.

items.label: Machine Authentication PAC
items.desc: Identifies a machine, for access when no user is logged in.

items.label: User Authorization PAC
items.desc: Identifies a user and carries authorization data; has no PAC-Key.
